content: 1. Encourage caregivers to engage in activities that involve giving their child objects to place into containers, take out, and stack. These activities are beneficial for the child’s skill development and should be continued at home. 2. If the child is nearing the end of their developmental age group or has already mastered age-appropriate activities, introduce activities suitable for the next developmental stage. 3. Before the caregiver and child leave, observe them performing the recommended play or communication activities to ensure the caregiver understands and can implement them. Encourage the caregiver to continue these activities at home and ask how they plan to do so. 4. Explain to the caregiver the importance of stimulating the child’s development. Highlight that play, communication, and proper feeding practices contribute to the child’s health, learning, and brain development, especially in the early years of life. 5. Emphasize that engaging in play and communication activities helps the child grow smarter, happier, and better prepared for school and future contributions to the family and community. 6. Help the caregiver build confidence in caring for their child by practicing play and communication activities together. Praise their efforts and provide specific feedback on how these activities benefit the child. 7. In role-play exercises, participants should practice advising caregivers. Assign roles such as caregiver, child, counselor, and observer. The counselor should select age-appropriate activities, guide the caregiver in engaging the child, and explain the benefits of these activities. 8. If the caregiver cannot breastfeed, advise them to hold the child close during feeding, maintain eye contact, and talk or sing to the child. Explain that while breastfeeding is ideal, children can thrive with proper care and attention during feeding. 9. If the caregiver is unsure about how to play or communicate with the child, demonstrate how the child responds to their actions. Encourage the caregiver to recognize the importance of play and communication for learning and to imitate the child’s sounds or gestures to foster interaction. 10. If the caregiver feels overwhelmed or stressed, listen to their concerns and help them identify someone who can support them. Build their confidence by demonstrating simple activities they can do with their child and offering praise for their efforts. 11. If the caregiver feels they lack time for play and communication, suggest combining these activities with daily caregiving tasks, such as feeding, bathing, or dressing. Encourage other family members to assist with chores or spend time with the child. 12. If the caregiver has no toys for the child, recommend using clean and safe household objects or making simple toys. Emphasize that children learn through play with people and objects, and store-bought toys are not necessary. 13. If the child is not responding or seems slow to develop, encourage the family to engage in extra play and communication activities. Check the child’s ability to see and hear, and refer them to specialized services if needed. 14. If the child has difficulty hearing or seeing, ask the caregiver specific questions to assess these abilities. For example, does the child turn their head toward sounds or follow moving objects with their eyes? If the answers suggest difficulties, refer the child for further assessment. 15. If the child has experienced the loss of a parent, help identify a special person who can provide love and attention. Explain that with good care, the child can recover from the loss and form new bonds over time. 16. If the caregiver treats the child harshly, recommend positive ways to manage behavior. Encourage the caregiver to praise the child for good behavior, respect the child’s feelings, and offer choices instead of saying “don’t.” Demonstrate how to redirect the child’s attention to appropriate activities. 17. When counseling caregivers, complete a checklist to document the advice given and problems discussed. Use this as a reference to ensure all aspects of the child’s development are addressed. 18. Discuss with facilitators or peers the specific needs of a child and their caregiver, and recommend activities tailored to their situation. For example, if a caregiver struggles to comfort the child, suggest looking into the child’s eyes, speaking gently, and holding the child to provide reassurance. 19. For children under six months, encourage caregivers to play by moving the baby’s arms and legs or gently stroking them. If the caregiver does not engage in play, discuss ways to stimulate the baby’s senses through age-appropriate activities. 20. For children six months and older, encourage caregivers to play and communicate with the child through activities that match their developmental stage. Help the caregiver interpret the child’s actions and responses, and guide them in fostering interaction and smiles. 21. If the child is slow to learn, demonstrate how the caregiver can respond to the child’s attempts to communicate. Encourage the caregiver to spend more time feeding, playing, and communicating with the child, as special attention can help the child learn, even if progress is slow. 22. If the child has special difficulties, such as hearing or vision problems, refer them to appropriate services for assessment and care. Regardless of the outcome, encourage the family to continue playing and communicating with the child to support their development. 23. Discuss with the caregiver how to integrate play and communication into daily routines and identify family members who can assist in providing care and attention to the child.
